caption:
Nvidia lost about $491 billion in market value in one session on Friday.
Reuters reported that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at the company.
The shares fell about 13 to 14 percent, after already sliding with the rest of AI stocks.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia shares fell about 13 percent on November 20, 2026, after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is examining the chipmaker's accounting. Reuters cited two people briefed on the matter and said enforcement staff are looking at potential accounting issues.

According to The Motley Fool, the stock dropped about 14 percent in the afternoon to less than $126, erasing roughly $491 billion in market value in a single session. That took Nvidia from about $3.52 trillion to about $3.03 trillion.
The shares were already down more than 6 percent earlier in the day amid a broad sell-off in AI stocks, both outlets reported. The Reuters report on the accounting focus deepened the slide.
What the SEC is reportedly examining

The Wall Street Journal reported on November 17 that the SEC was investigating Nvidia but could not determine the focus of the probe, according to Reuters. Reuters said it could not establish when the SEC opened its inquiry or which specific accounting practices are under review. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment, and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reuters pointed to two areas that have drawn attention. The first is how Nvidia reports revenue by region. Last year the company began assigning sales to the location of a customer's headquarters instead of its billing address, and Singapore was removed from its geographic breakdown. The Financial Times reported on November 17, citing company accounts, that Singapore-billed sales had climbed to almost half of global revenue.
The Motley Fool noted that under the headquarters method, about 63 percent of last quarter's revenue came from customers based in the United States.

The second area is customer financing. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and has provided guarantees tied to data center projects, Reuters said. On the company's earnings call on November 17, interim chief executive Colette Kress said the guarantees totaled $118 billion at the end of the quarter, including $105 billion of credit support tied to a single data center campus, according to The Motley Fool. Kress also said Nvidia would be far more selective about AI industry financing deals going forward.

Reuters noted that investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and that many end without enforcement action. SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said last month that the agency was examining disclosures by AI companies, and the SEC recently created a financial reporting and accounting unit inside its enforcement division, Reuters reported.

The probe adds to a difficult month for Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive on November 11 after revelations about his personal relationships, including with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. China denies that she is a spy. Kress, the former chief financial officer, now leads the company on an interim basis.

The Justice Department is also reviewing Nvidia's $12.9 billion deal to buy Hugging Face as part of a broader antitrust investigation, Reuters reported last month. Reuters said Nvidia shares have fallen more than a third since the crisis began.

The Motley Fool put the drawdown at about 48 percent from the record close of $239.24 on October 6, or about $2.7 trillion in market value lost in six weeks. The business itself is still growing quickly: revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion last quarter, and the company expects about $130 billion this quarter.

The gap between those results and the share price shows how much of Nvidia's value now depends on trust in its numbers and its leadership rather than on demand for its chips. Questions about where revenue is booked and how much customer spending Nvidia itself supports go to the core of that trust, even if the inquiry ends without charges.

The next signal is whether Nvidia or the SEC confirms the scope of the inquiry and which accounting practices it covers. Any change to how Nvidia reports regional revenue or customer guarantees in its next filing would also show how seriously the company is treating the questions.
